newsitem.title: USA: Florida city calm night after riot.
newsitem.headline: Florida city calm night after riot.

text.p: Calm prevailed on Friday night on the streets of mainly black inner-city neighborhoods where residents had rioted 24 hours earlier after a white policeman shot dead a black motorist.
"We are very relieved calm has prevailed into the dark hours," Police Chief Darrell Stephens told reporters.

There was a heavy police presence throughout the area, with police cars patrolling the streets and others stationed at intersections. Officers wore helmets, flak jackets and carried shotguns, but Stephens said only two incidents had been reported.

One involved a person throwing a bottle at a police car and the other involved two fires being set in dumpsters. "It could be any Friday night. On a normal Friday night there might be more arrests," Stephens said.

Earlier, city officials had declared a state of emergency and temporarily halted handgun sales to try to maintain calm in neighborhoods where angry crowds on Thursday had set fires and pelted police with rocks and bottles after the shooting.
"There is reason to believe that a clear and present danger exists of a riot or other general public disorder," said a declaration issued by Mayor David Fischer and the police department.
Some 200 National Guardsmen were on stand-by at a city athletic stadium in case violence broke out after nightfall.
The emergency order banned the sale and display of firearms and ammunition, and banned carrying firearms in public. It also prohibited the sale of gasoline except when put directly into a vehicle.

Roderick Pringles, brother of the motorist shot dead by a police officer on Thursday evening, appealed to the community to remain calm. Pringles said the police officer was wrong to have opened fire on his brother, but said the rioting that followed had not accomplished anything.
"I guess people were looking for something to blame on somebody and that was it," he told reporters at a news conference on the steps of city hall in St. Petersburg.

In Washington, a Justice Department spokesman said the Federal Bureau of Investigation had launched a preliminary civil rights inquiry into motorist Tyrone Lewis's death and the department's Community Relations Service sent conflict-resolution experts to the scene to help ease tensions.
Police said that Lewis, 18, had a warrant outstanding for his arrest but they were unable to say on what charge.
The state of emergency and emergency actions were to remain in place until late Monday afternoon.

Local officials acknowledged tensions between black youths and police in the slow-paced city on Florida's Gulf Coast -- home to a large number of elderly and retired -- but Stephens said, "The city remains calm."
"The streets are open, people are moving freely about. We hope we can keep that calm through the weekend as we begin to work on the longer term problems," he said.

Stephens, Fischer, Florida Gov. Lawton Chiles and other officials held a two-hour meeting with black community leaders on Friday and said it had gone well and a broad range of issues had been addressed.

"We wanted them to pour out what their feelings were," Fischer said after the meeting. "I'm very disappointed this happened because we thought we were doing real well. We have work to do. I'm surprised and disappointed, but we are realists and you can't change everything in four years. We can't change the situation with jobs or housing overnight."
Some black residents said they were angry and blamed police not only for the shooting death but also for the hours of brick-throwing, looting and arson that followed.
At least 28 fires were set by arsonists during the rioting, 11 people were injured and 20 people had been arrested.

The incident began at about 7:30 p.m. EDT (2330 GMT) on Thursday when two police officers, a white male and white female, stopped Lewis for speeding in a neighborhood with a history of trouble with drug dealers, police said.

They shot him because they believed he was trying to run them down, police said. But some witnesses said the driver had done nothing to prompt the shooting, although Stephens denied rumors that Lewis was shot when he was out of his car with his hands in the air.
The riot began shortly afterward at the intersection of 18th Avenue South and 16th Street South, where the shooting took place.
